notes.text: Kannada writes almost exactly as it sounds. Learn the letters once and you can read a signboard anywhere.
Namaskara is the polite one. Between friends people just say enu samachara, or simply oh, banni: come in.
Respect lives in the verb here. Nivu banni to an elder, nee baa to a friend. Same word, different ending.
Anna and akka mean elder brother and sister, but strangers get them too. Age decides the word, not blood.
Uta means a full rice meal, tindi means a snack or breakfast. Asking which one you had matters.
Counting stops at lakSha and koTi, not million. A crore is one koTi, and everyone reads prices that way.
Colour words end in bannu: kempu bannu, red colour. Kempu also names a person, and half of old Bengaluru.
Bengaluru means town of boiled beans. Ooru is any hometown, so hogona ooru kade means let us go home.
Nale means tomorrow and monne means day before yesterday. Kannada keeps single words for days English needs three for.
Bargaining starts with swalpa kammi madi: make it a little less. Swalpa, a little, softens almost any request.
Hushar means both clever and healthy. Asking hushara means are you well, and complimenting a sharp child too.
Mane is house, but manetanaa means running a household. Kannada builds long words by stacking small ones together.
Kelasa covers job, task and chore alike. Kelasa ide, I have work, politely ends any conversation you want out of.
Feelings sit in the mind here: mansige bejaar, sadness to the mind. You do not have sad, sadness comes to you.
Ugadi is new year, from yuga and adi, age plus beginning. You eat neem and jaggery, bitter with sweet.
